title: Result with Match
story: You're writing a file uploader. Uploads can succeed (file saved) or fail (disk full, permission denied, network timeout). Each outcome needs different handling — match gives you the power to handle every scenario.
why: Match on Result gives you complete control over both success and failure paths — you can print, retry, log, or transform based on which outcome you get.
analogy: Match on Result is like a fork in the road — one path leads to the celebration (Ok), the other to the repair shop (Err). You're prepared for either destination.
try_it: Add another validation rule: reject emails shorter than 5 characters with Err("Email too short"). Does your match still handle all cases correctly? Test with "a@b" and "user@site.com".
tips: Match branches can contain multiple statements — use braces `{ }` for multi-line arms
Return early from inside a match arm if needed — it returns from the enclosing function
Name your error strings thoughtfully — they're for humans to read and understand what went wrong
common_mistakes: Only checking Ok and ignoring Err — the compiler won't let you, but conceptually you should have meaningful error handling
Returning from one match arm but not the other when the match is the last expression of a function
Using match when an `if let` would be cleaner — if you only handle Ok, consider if let Ok(x) = result
